title: Being Special is Overrated
author: Arthur Brooks
summary: In this weekly newsletter piece, Arthur Brooks argues that many high-performing people have developed an addiction to specialness -- to winning, to success, to being recognized as exceptional -- and that this addiction trades their genuine happiness for the dopamine rush of achievement. Drawing on his own birthday reflection, Brooks observes that people who prefer to be 'special' rather than 'happy' fall into a trap: success mimics addiction by stimulating dopamine, by causing people to sacrifice relationships and presence for performance, and by producing withdrawal symptoms (depression, anxiety) when it ends. The cure, he argues, is not abandoning achievement but redefining success: away from worldly rewards of money, power, and prestige (which depend on social comparison and deplete life satisfaction) and toward the intensity of love, the strength of one's philosophical or religious life, and how work serves others. The piece pairs with his Free Press column on commencement speeches, which is paywalled but referenced here.
points: * The preference for being 'special' over being 'happy' is a pervasive but insidious trap: people who are wired this way often can't celebrate birthdays or ordinary joys because they're measuring against a standard of exceptional achievement rather than ordinary flourishing. * Success addiction has the neurological and behavioral fingerprints of real addiction: praise stimulates dopamine (implicated in all addictive behaviors), people sacrifice relationships and presence for career gains (missing recitals, forgoing marriage), and those who step back from achievement suffer withdrawal in the form of depression and anxiety. * Social comparison is the engine of success addiction -- research is clear that measuring yourself by worldly rewards relative to others strips life satisfaction -- and the only escape is to redefine the success metric entirely. * Brooks's three practical steps are: say out loud 'I will never find true happiness by forgoing my happiness'; start showing up to life (choose the ballet recital over the board meeting); and redefine success by the intensity of love, the strength of one's religious or philosophical life, and how work serves others. * The research on post-Olympic athletes is striking: depression and anxiety are common after elite athletic careers end, showing that even the highest-performing achievers experience withdrawal from specialness -- a reminder that the pursuit of distinction is a machine that can never be satisfied.
quotes: My birthday was last week. I've always had trouble celebrating, not because I fear getting older, but because, well, what exactly is so special about having a birthday? Literally everybody in the world has one every single year. Maybe you think this is weird, in which case, you are normal. But maybe you think this is normal, in which case you are weird, like me. If so, you probably fall prey to a common but insidious type of thinking: you prefer to be special rather than happy.

Though it isn't a conventional medical addiction, for many people, specialness in the form of winning or success has addictive properties. To a certain extent, I mean that literally -- praise stimulates the neurotransmitter dopamine, which is implicated in all addictive behaviors.

But success also resembles addiction in its effect on human relationships. People sacrifice their links with others for their truest love, success. They travel for business on anniversaries; miss Little League games and recitals while working long hours. Some forgo marriage for their careers -- even though a good marriage brings more happiness than any job.

Success addicts trying to kick their habit experience withdrawal as well. Research finds that depression and anxiety are common among elite athletes after their careers end; Olympic athletes, in particular, suffer from the 'post-Olympic blues.' I saw this withdrawal all the time in my years as the president of a think tank in Washington, D.C., a city in which prominent people in politics and media would step back from the limelight and suffer greatly.

Redefine success. If you measure yourself only by the worldly rewards of money, power, and prestige, you'll spend all your life comparing yourself to others. It's time to redefine success by the intensity of love in your life; by the strength of your religious or philosophical life; and by how your work serves others -- not by the worldly rewards you've earned.
